Once summer is over, the Polish capital buttons back up. Laura Studarus/Handout/Supplied Share Save for later Please log in to bookmark this story. Log In Create Free Account It’s 5 p.m. on Aug. 1, and the entire area around Warsaw’s Rondo Dmowskiego roundabout has come to a halt. Sirens sound; hordes of motorcyclists begin revving their engines. Head bowed, locals hold up smoke sticks, creating a “fog of war” effect. This is a celebration of “W” Hour, a one-minute remembrance of the heroes of the 1944 Warsaw Uprising, a 63-day act of military resistance to Nazi occupation that ended with much of the city being destroyed. It’s also a compelling reminder that Warsaw is a city still finding ways to embrace the future while honouring its past. I’ve spent every summer in Warsaw for the past decade. While my primary motivation for the repeated visits is seeing the friends I’ve made over the years, I’ve also fallen in love with the city’s rapid evolution. And while locals leaving the city to take one last vacation before the return of autumn weather will disagree with me, August is the best time to visit Warsaw. Open this photo in gallery: A young resident holds up a smoke stick as part of Aug. 1 ‘W’ Hour ceremonies in Warsaw. Laura Studarus/Handout/Supplied The unofficial theme of the month is getting outdoors. It isn’t just the café owners dragging their tables onto the sidewalks (although spots in Savior Square could certainly give Paris a run for its money). There are simply more opportunities for outdoor socialization during the summer. Once summer is over, Warsaw buttons back up. I am not a morning person, but I will start my August weekends by dragging myself out of bed for the breakfast market Targ Śniadaniowy , a summer event which sets up shop in the Żoliborz neighbourhood on Saturdays, and the Mokotów area on Sundays. Evening owls will appreciate Nocny Market , a night market that repurposes the abandoned platforms of Warszawa Gtowna train station on the weekends. Both events showcase Warsaw’s ever-expanding bench of international food options, art and music. My favourite places: A local filmmaker’s guide to London’s parks and cycling trails A caveat on visiting Warsaw’s Old Town: The neighbourhood was fully destroyed in the Second World War. While the buildings that stand there now are beautiful, they’re a recreation of what it looked like – one that comes with overpriced restaurants. But I’ll make an exception for Jazz na Starowce , a summer-long jazz festival that’s taken residence in the colourful square for the past 32 years. Open this photo in gallery: The music of Chopin endures in live Sunday performances in Lazienki Park. Laura Studarus/Handout/Supplied But if you’re looking for more local-approved food and culture, grab bowls at Bar Pacyfik and bring them to LOT’s Summer Cinema series, an outdoor movie showing held in the shadow of the Palace of Culture on Tuesday, Thursdays, and Saturdays. Or picnic in Lazienki Park on Sundays with the accompaniment of a live Chopin piano concert series. One of Warsaw’s most famous creatives may have passed more than 170 years ago, but the long shadow of Chopin’s legacy can also be felt at Pardon, To Tu , a bar that often books local free jazz, classical and improvisational artists. The area around the Vistula River isn’t excessively built out, and that’s exactly why I like it. Along the Praga side, the banks are largely left as is, acting as an ad hoc nature preserve. (Translation: Bring bug spray.) However, on the Warsaw side, the Vistula Boulevards, a six-kilometre strip running along the river, populated by skaters, walkers and joggers, can be a particularly enjoyable place to sit in the sun during the day. This is especially true if you take up residence on one of Warsaw’s many artificial beaches. But the area comes alive at night. Floating establishments – like the aptly named BarKa – offer both drinks and evening concerts, turning the area into a shockingly well-behaved open-air bar. (Just don’t try to drink in other parts of the city – consuming alcohol in parks and streets will result in a fine.) The city has continued to pour money into this area, including opening the Ktadka walking bridge in 2024, which has become one of my favourite spots to watch the sunset. I’m a walker regardless of location, but on Sundays in the summer, Nowy Swiat and Krakowskie Przedmiescie – two streets that wind through Warsaw’s high-end shopping district and into Castle Square – go car-free. Here, the experience of strolling the streets, or just stopping for a traditional Polish doughnut (with twists such as Nutella and passion fruit) at Dobra Pączkarnia Warszawa , becomes all the more inviting. Open this photo in gallery: When riding one of the old trams on a summer weekend, buy tickets in advance or risk being fined. Laura Studarus/Handout/Supplied Public transit sightseers, the city has you as well – on the weekends during the summer, special trams from the 1940s and 1950s run along Line T . It’s delightful enough to see the candy-coloured cars rattle by, but passengers are also taken on a route that includes Filtrowa Street, the Warsaw Uprising Museum and Wola cemeteries – considered to be some of the most compelling points of interest in the city. Unlike their more modern tram car relatives, these don’t have ticket machines on board, so be sure to purchase a ticket at a nearby subway station or on a mobile app, or risk being that North American unsuccessfully trying to talk your way out of a stiff fine. (Trust me, it doesn’t work.) A ski holiday in Poland? A visit to the wild alpine fun of Zakopane August in Warsaw may start with a sombre remembrance, but the month is ultimately a celebration. The Polish capital is still in the middle of a decades-long rebuilding process, but they’ve found a balance – one that allows for both memory and progress. Just be sure to take it all in before the mercury drops. If you go Open this photo in gallery: Old Town Warsaw: A reconstruction of pre-Second World War buildings, but built on history nevertheless. Laura Studarus/Handout/Supplied Poland’s national carrier LOT is the only airline that offers regular non-stop flights between Toronto and Warsaw. If you choose to add Warsaw on to a larger European trip, be sure to book your flights into Warsaw Chopin (WAW) rather than Warsaw Modlin (WMI), to save transit times into the city. Embrace the city’s past and modernist future by staying at Hotel Warszawa , a formal Second World War target turned five-star hotel. It celebrates Warsaw’s past with a modernist design that showcases the building’s original materials and scars. The location also provides an incredible view of the Palace of Culture. Poland uses Polish ztoty . While most stores and restaurants across Warsaw accept credit cards and Apple Pay, it’s worth keeping cash handy. You’ll want funds for park ice-cream vendors and milk bars – low-cost kitchens serving traditional Polish food. Because August is a month of remembrance, the Warsaw Uprising Museum often sells out weeks in advance and requires advance reservations. Likewise, the award-winning POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews , regularly considered one of the best museums in Europe, is worth booking ahead if you have a preferred time of visit. The majority of museums in Warsaw also offer one free day every week . The writer’s hotel stay was complimentary and it did not review or approve this article. Beállítom Letartóztattak a horvátországi Pula városban egy ukrán búvárt, akit a német hatóságok az Északi Áramlat felrobbantásával gyanúsítanak – közölte a német szövetségi ügyészség. A közleményükben Vladimir Z. néven említett férfi az ügyészség szerint „egy képzett búvár, aki tagja volt azon személyek csoportjának, akik robbanószereket helyeztek el az Északi Áramlat 1 és az Északi Áramlat 2 földgázvezetékein a dániai Bornholm-sziget közelében 2022 szeptemberében”. A férfit az ügyészség közlése szerint a horvát rendőrség segítségével tartóztatták le egy európai letartóztatási parancs alapján. Az index.hr című horvát lap szerda kora délután azt írta , hogy a horvát rendőrség egyelőre nem jelentette be a férfi letartóztatását. A német ügyészség közölte, hogy kérvényezték a férfi kiadatását. A dpa német hírügynökség cikke szerint ugyanarról, a korábban Volodimir Zsuravljov néven említett férfiról van szó, akit tavaly szeptemberben Lengyelországban már letartóztattak. A férfi kiadatását Németországnak végül egy lengyel bíróság elutasította , arra hivatkozva, hogy a németek alig indokolták meg a kiadatást, valamint hogy az ukránok „igazságos, védekező háborút” vívnak, aminek során az ellenség infrastruktúráját támadták. Ezt Donald Tusk lengyel kormányfő is támogatta. Tavaly nyáron Olaszországban vettek őrizetbe egy ukrán férfit, akit pár hónappal később kiadtak Németországnak, ahol az ügyészek július elején vádat emeltek ellene a gázvezetékek felrobbantása miatt. A német ügyészség közölte azt is, hogy Szerhij K., aki akkor az ukrán hadsereg tisztje volt, más katonákkal együtt „ az ukrán állami hatóságok parancsára ” dolgozta ki az Északi Áramlat 1 és 2 gázvezetékek megsemmisítésére irányuló tervet. Az Északi Áramlat gázvezetéket 2022 szeptemberében robbantották fel. A Wall Street Journal két évvel később az ukrán vezetést nevezte meg az Északi Áramlat gázvezeték felrobbantásának értelmi szerzőjeként és végrehajtójaként, azután, hogy Németország körözést adott ki egy ukrán állampolgárral szemben, aki részt vehetett az akcióban. A 2022-es támadás lényegesen korlátozta az Európába irányuló orosz gázszállítást. Az akciót, ami komoly eszkalációt jelentett az orosz–ukrán háborúban, a nyugati országok és Oroszország is szabotázsként írták le. Senki nem vállalta érte a felelősséget, Ukrajna tagadja, hogy köze lenne hozzá. Később arról írt a lap, hogy német nyomozók szerint egy elit ukrán katonai egység hajtotta végre a támadásokat Ukrajna akkori legfőbb parancsnoka, Valerij Zaluzsnij tábornok közvetlen felügyelete alatt. https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/22/emma.text: Menü Kereső Macron: Oroszország terrorral igyekszik megtörni Ukrajnát, de ez nem fog sikerülni Külföld Bakró-Nagy Ferenc Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Megdöbbenését és a felháborodását fejezte ki a francia elnök Zelenszkijnek egy telefonbeszélgetés során a pénteken a közép-ukrajnai Krivij Rih városát ért támadás miatt – posztolt erről Emmanuel Macron az X-en. A francia elnök szerint a civilek támadásával Oroszország az eszkaláció útjára lép, valószínűleg erőfitogtatásra törekszik, de leginkább csak a gyengeségét árulja el. „Emiatt elengedhetetlen, hogy Ukrajnának minden szükséges eszközt biztosítsunk légterének védelméhez és az agresszió megakadályozásához” – írta Macron, és közölte, hogy megerősítik támogatásukat: elfogórakétákat szállítanak Ukrajnának, és tovább folytatják együttműködésüket a tavaly aláírt szándéknyilatkozat szerint. A francia elnök elengedhetetlennek nevezte, hogy minden olyan ország, amely rendelkezik az ehhez szükséges képességekkel, csatlakozzon. „Tovább kell fokoznunk az Oroszországra nehezedő nyomást, amíg nem hajlandóak beszüntetni a harcokat és békét kötni” – írta. „Oroszország terrorral igyekszik megtörni Ukrajnát, de ez nem fog sikerülni. Ukrajnával szolidárisak maradva gondoskodni fogunk arról, hogy a jog és az igazság felülkerekedjen az erőszakon” – zárta posztját Emmanuel Macron. Pénteken orosz drónok csapódtak be egy bevásárlóközpontba a közép-ukrajnai Krivij Rih városában, a helyi hatóságok szerint legalább 15-en meghaltak, több mint 130-an pedig megsebesültek, köztük 23 gyerek. Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök szülővárosára fényes nappal mértek csapást, a támadást X-en cinikusnak és aljasnak nevezte, valamint felszólította a világot, hogy vonják felelősségre Oroszországot. Mint írta, hogy a drónok két hullámban csaptak le: az első találat után nagyjából fél órával egy második csapás következett, ami szerinte arra utal, hogy szándékosan a mentőket vették célba. Az ukrán elnök egy későbbi posztjában közölte, hogy mindenképpen válaszlépéseket tesznek. Kapcsolódó Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Kövess minket Facebookon is! (AP Photo/Konstantin Toropin) (Konstantin Toropin/AP Photo/Konstantin Toropin) By KONSTANTIN TOROPIN, Associated Press August 30, 2026 at 8:25 pm EDT HOHENFELS, Germany — On a moonless and rainy night, a group of soldiers emerged from a ramshackle building meant to resemble a church. The alpine terrain loomed over them as they quietly set off for the tree line of the German countryside a short distance away. The soldiers are members of the Polish special forces and are taking part in an exercise designed only months ago that simulates moving through enemy lines, traversing miles of enemy territory and launching a drone strike on a key enemy location . Initially designed by the Army's Green Berets for U.S. special forces, the exercise that began Friday is informed by and simulates many of the challenges that Ukrainian troops have experienced in their conflict with Russia . It is the first time a NATO ally like Poland has undertaken the training, and it comes at a time when tensions between Russian President Vladimir Putin and NATO countries have escalated . “We’re using lessons learned from Ukraine,” an Army Green Beret officer assigned to the training complex said Thursday. “All of those effects that we’re seeing either Russia or Ukraine having to overcome — we’re doing our best to replicate.” The Associated Press received rare access to both the training ground and the troops conducting the exercise, which has only been conducted twice before, both times this year, by two different Green Beret teams. The drill highlights the focus that some parts of the U.S. military have on learning the latest techniques in drone warfare , pioneered by Ukraine during its 4 1/2-year effort to repel Russian forces. It also shows how the U.S., its NATO allies and Ukraine are working together to counter the threat of possible further Russian action in coming years even as the Trump administration has warned of troop drawdowns in Europe . CIA Director John Ratcliffe went to Moscow this week to warn Russia not to attack NATO countries, The Wall Street Journal reported . Russia has the appetite to conduct sabotage and cyberattacks against NATO countries, but Putin wants to avoid a direct confrontation , according to three Western officials, who spoke Friday on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters. How special forces are learning to sneak behind enemy lines to deploy drones During the exercise in Germany, a senior enlisted soldier familiar with the training scenario at Joint Multinational Readiness Center Hohenfels — about an hour's drive southeast from Nuremberg — said the plan is to run it several times a year. The officer said he expects most, if not all, of the 32 NATO nations to express interest in sending their troops to try the exercise. Both spoke on condition of anonymity in line with the U.S. military's longstanding policy of not publicly identifying individual members of special forces units. The scenario, which runs for several days, takes place on a large, 1,100-square-mile (3,000-square-kilometer) plot of land nestled in the Bavarian countryside. Poland's special forces will be expected to sneak past a U.S. Army airborne infantry unit, whose soldiers will play the enemy. The U.S. airborne infantry unit will parachute into the closed-off training area at the Army's Hohenfels base and set themselves up into a front line. Assuming the Polish forces can make their way past the U.S. Army, they must then move north — through about 60 miles (100 kilometers) of German countryside — to another training area in the town of Grafenwoehr, where they are expected to destroy a simulated target. In between lie German farms and villages, private and government cameras, as well as a city with a large population, all of which not only pose as obstacles but also create the potential for them to be spotted. The senior enlisted soldier said that in previous instances of the exercise, the Army Green Berets removed their uniforms “so they can blend in” before adding that “blend in also means don’t get seen by civilians.” German civilians in the area largely are not aware of the exercise and serve as a reasonable test of how well special forces can blend into the local population. If they fail, reports of suspicious people to police will make it back to the military, which will use them to pinpoint the team. “This is supposed to be Russia and you’re going to stand out in Russia,” the enlisted soldier added. Plus, the U.S. Army also will be looking for the Polish forces with drones of their own. If they're spotted, “now you have the entire Russian arsenal coming at you,” the enlisted soldier said. The U.S. Army can either send a military police unit to hunt for the Polish special forces with dogs or direct more drones to the area. In previous versions of the exercise, the U.S. Army had access to more than a hundred drones, the enlisted soldier said. Troops are able to be “captured or killed” as part of the training. Countries seek help from Ukraine on drone warfare While the exercise taps into drones and NATO teamwork, the message of collaboration and the value of drones has been somewhat mixed lately across the military. President Donald Trump stirred confusion among NATO allies by going back and forth on drawing down U.S. troop levels in Europe, and the administration has launched a force review on next steps. And last week, the Army's top officer shuttered a unit that specialized in drone warfare. But overall, there is growing interest in tapping Ukraine for its expertise on modern warfare and, specifically, drones. In March, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was helping five countries in the Middle East and Gulf region counter Iranian drone attacks launched during the war with the United States, while the U.S. and European countries were among those requesting support. Meanwhile, the number of mysterious drone incursions in Europe have grown, including as recently as this month, when a pair of drones were spotted over a German military base and a drone carrying explosives was found at a key cargo airport in Germany. ___ Associated Press writer Emma Burrows in London contributed to this report.
